utterances.speaker: B

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, that's a great question. I guess there's really two paths. I mean, I think there's like— there's definitely like a phenomenon we're seeing even in the atmosphere where, you know, now that, you know, cloud code exists and it's much easier to build web apps and ship things, there's something I feel like a lot of folks are not really thinking about the design side of things. What you end up seeing is like user interfaces that look very, very similar. Like you go to one website and it looks the same as the next. And so like if you're in that boat, you're not trying to like actually go deep on design, like I think there's some very practical things that you can learn to, you know, help steer these tools in the right direction so that the things that you are creating better reflect your own unique style or tastes or things, and they don't just end up looking like vanilla whatever comes out of the thing. Whereas if you actually want to go deep into design, I mean, I think a lot of that stuff hasn't changed. I mean, I think it's— you have to be, you know, reading books. You have to be looking at some of the great designers of the past, and that work is still incredibly relevant. And I think, you know, for me, it's a big part of the process is just regularly consuming good art and good design and letting that sort of absorb into my brain and influence me. Because it's kind of— it's very ambiguous feeling. It's not like a very— like, it's not a switch you can flip. It just takes a lot of, like, consuming lots of good content and good ideas and design so that on the other end, something— your own unique take on things flows out on the other end.
